kp.k: Legal AI needs public performance evidence
kp.d: This 2026 perspective argues that legal AI lacks 'legibility': sufficient, accurate and representative public benchmarking information about deployed systems. The authors distinguish this problem from model interpretability and developer transparency. Their contribution is an institutional analysis and recommendations, rather than a new empirical measurement of legal AI performance.
qs: We argue that there is a need for public AI benchmarking in law.
In contrast, we offer an insti- tutional perspective (21, 22).
Illegibility can arise because public information is insuﬀicient, inaccurate, or unrepresentative.

kp.k: Benchmark design determines what performance claims mean
kp.d: The authors identify six discretionary dimensions: task definition, benchmark construction, evaluation protocol, measurements, system selection and transparency. Narrow tasks or unrepresentative samples can exaggerate usefulness; inconsistent prompting and configurations undermine comparisons. They cite a cross-domain example in which Gemini's reported advantage over GPT-4 disappeared under standardized conditions.
qs: Selecting those tasks requires attention to users’ informational needs and the range of real-world applications.
Construction decisions shape benchmark diﬀiculty (28)
Standardized protocols can reveal that purported improvements vanish or that com- peting systems perform roughly equally.

kp.k: Reported accuracy depends on benchmark difficulty and disclosure
kp.d: The paper reports that an academic study found a Thomson Reuters legal research tool hallucinated in 33% of benchmark queries, whereas the company subsequently reported an internal error rate of 10%. The authors say construction differences may explain the discrepancy but cannot determine this without the company's benchmark information. They also criticize Paxton AI's 94%+ accuracy claim for using an unusually easy explicit-overruling task, rather than demonstrating broader case-treatment reliability.
qs: hallucinated in 33% of benchmark queries (6).
its own internal measurement of error rate of 10%
Paxton AI achieves 94%+ accuracy
that even simple bag-of-words models achieve near-perfect performance.

kp.d: The authors recommend disaggregating performance by question type, legal field, jurisdiction and other relevant subgroups. They argue that assessments may need to consider worst-case outcomes as well as averages. Success criteria also depend on the application: tenant-facing advice requires tone, clarity and emotional appropriateness alongside correctness, while contracts and summaries lack universally accepted quality metrics.
qs: Benchmarking also requires deciding what aspects of performance to assess.
This depends on context-specific values and use cases.
Benchmarking in these instances must navigate both normative uncertainty and practical ambiguity about what constitutes success.

kp.k: Transparency creates contamination and gaming tradeoffs
kp.d: Publishing benchmark data supports scrutiny and methodological improvement but can permit intentional training on tests or inadvertent contamination through web-scraped training data. Replacing exposed benchmarks raises costs. As a cross-domain illustration of institutional bias, the authors report that Chatbot Arena gave preferred providers opportunities to test variants privately and disclose only their best results.
qs: Transparency implicates major tradeoﬀs.
Yet transparency also creates risks of gaming that can erode the validity of the benchmark.
allowing them to privately test many model variants and publicly release only their best-performing versions (40).

kp.k: Human interaction affects legal AI's practical value
kp.d: The paper emphasizes benchmarking human–AI collaboration as well as standalone systems because many tools augment rather than replace lawyers. It argues that output-checking and second-guessing can erode the value of an otherwise accurate system. Beyond a handful of studies and anecdotal reporting, the authors find limited knowledge about actual professional usage and its effects on accuracy, efficiency and error.
qs: The lack of information also extends to how humans interact with legal AI.
we generally know little about how legal professionals actually use AI tools in practice
or how human– AI collaboration aﬀects accuracy, eﬀiciency, and error.

kp.k: Legal benchmarking requires costly, contextual expert judgment
kp.d: Legal generative tasks frequently require manual assessment by trained legal annotators, sometimes multiple annotators to accommodate subjective disagreement. Jurisdictional variation and changing law complicate representative testing: eviction advice can differ across counties and years. The authors also contrast law's emphasis on process and effort with medicine's institutionalized measurement of outcomes. These constraints limit system coverage and evaluation frequency.
qs: This makes benchmarking costly, as trained legal annotators are expensive.
Legal AI also has more tasks which are “subjective,” and for which quality may be contested (15).
Answers might also change over time, based on updates to the law (through statutes, regulations, or case law).

kp.k: Vendor incentives can compromise public benchmarking
kp.d: The authors argue that vendors possess resources and technical expertise but face sales incentives to favor their own products through task selection, sample distributions, protocols, aggregate metrics and selective version reporting. Confidentiality can also limit their knowledge of actual usage. They describe existing governance as focused primarily on practitioners' uses of AI rather than product-level testing or disclosure requirements.
qs: vendors are primarily motivated by- product sales
Vendors might define tasks narrowly around areas where their systems perform well
Yet legal AI currently lacks this kind of product-centered governance.

kp.k: Purchaser collaboration risks unequal access and influence
kp.d: Law firms and other purchasers can contribute realistic usage information but may treat benchmarking knowledge as a competitive asset. Consortia could pool costs, expertise and infrastructure, yet differing resources could create separate rich and poor groups or preferential access for larger contributors. The authors warn that resulting benchmarks could prioritize major firms' transactional work over solo practitioners and public-interest needs.
qs: A central challenge here is the risk of rent-seeking.
Because purchasers are often in competition with one another, they have strong incentives to treat benchmarking information as a proprietary asset.
Members who contribute more (in capital, com- pute, or expertise) might receive more or better information

kp.k: Independent institutions face access and capacity barriers
kp.d: Academics and nonprofits may offer independence but lack funding, representative usage data, commercial-system access and comprehensive legal materials. Publication incentives favor novel benchmarks over repeated maintenance and can expose tests to contamination. Governance bodies have public-interest advantages but generally lack technical expertise and resources for comprehensive benchmarking. These are institutional constraints identified by the authors, not measured rankings of individual organizations.
qs: Important institutional legal data are often sur- prisingly privatized, unpublished, or inaccessible (69).
Finally, for academics, benchmarking may come with decreasing marginal returns.
Most notably, gov- ernments lack AI expertise and resources.

kp.k: Information gaps impede innovation and professional responsibility
kp.d: The authors argue that scarce performance information prevents developers from learning cumulatively, complicates responsible procurement and makes it difficult for lawyers to calibrate reliance to professional competence obligations. It also weakens legal education about effective AI use. They suggest that limited tool-specific evidence may help explain coarse disclosure rules that treat AI usage alike regardless of function or context.
qs: Third, illegibility can hamper legal education.
Finally, illegibility hinders governance.
These mandates rely on a crude distinction between AI and non-AI tools

kp.k: High-resource benchmarking should be independent and recurring
kp.d: For institutions with substantial financial, technical and legal resources, the authors propose an independent in-house benchmarking program covering diverse tasks and systems, repeated regularly, for example annually. NIST's facial-recognition evaluations, conducted since 1994, provide an analogy rather than evidence of an existing equivalent legal program. The proposal uses private test data to limit gaming and requires resources that the authors say current institutions may lack.
qs: For the high-resource setting, we suggest an independent and self-contained benchmark- ing eﬀort styled after NIST’s FRVT.
It would repeat benchmarking regularly
benchmarking in each succes- sive iteration has grown in breadth and complexity.

kp.k: Medium-resource consortia should divide institutional responsibilities
kp.d: At approximately an order of magnitude below the high-resource setting, the authors propose coordination across oversight bodies, academics, purchasers and developers. Oversight bodies would help select tasks; academics would design construction and evaluation procedures; purchasers would supply funding and legal expertise; developers would offer technical support. MLPerf and the legal track of TREC provide models. Risks include firm capture, inconsistent standards, publication embargoes to discourage free-riding and declining participation incentives.
qs: MLPerf serves as an inspiration for this model (77).
Bar associations might oﬀer Continuing Legal Education credit for lawyers who assist in the eﬀort.
Law firms will only participate if the tasks and systems evaluated are relevant to their activities.

kp.k: Low-resource efforts should prioritize access to justice
kp.d: At an order of magnitude below the medium-resource setting, the authors recommend targeted grants for narrowly scoped benchmarks or evaluations of a few systems. They prioritize tools used by people unable to assess quality themselves, including general-purpose chatbots consulted for bankruptcy, housing or child-custody questions. This is explicitly a triage recommendation: poor systems could harm vulnerable users, while effective ones could expand legal assistance, but targeted research cannot provide comprehensive market coverage.
qs: limited resources necessitates precision about which kinds of performance information are most useful.
ordinary users have far fewer resources, expertise, or institutional support to assess system quality.
But if they prove eﬀective, such tools could substantially expand access to legal assistance

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Guha and coauthors present cheaper and more accessible legal services as AI's promise, but argue that inadequate public performance information obstructs responsible adoption, innovation, procurement, education, and governance.
pts.d: The authors describe conversational legal research systems as intended to replace or augment keyword-based research, rather than claiming that lawyers themselves are being replaced. They argue that actual benefits depend on system reliability and human interaction: time spent checking or second-guessing outputs can diminish practical value even when a system performs well in isolation. Their central institutional claim is that legal AI lacks 'legibility'—public, representative performance information—and that this impedes cumulative technical improvement and informed professional reliance. They further argue that benchmark design and access can influence competition: evaluating only established products can disadvantage smaller vendors, while proprietary benchmarking can give law firms a competitive advantage. They propose resource-dependent public benchmarking arrangements, not a single universally optimal institution. For consumer-facing legal AI, they predict either harm to vulnerable users if tools perform poorly or substantially expanded legal assistance if tools prove effective.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article offers an institutional synthesis supported by earlier empirical studies, reported court incidents, vendor statements, and cross-domain benchmarking examples; it does not report a new empirical test of legal AI.
pts.d: For reliability concerns, the authors cite the Magesh et al. legal-research-tool study associated with Stanford RegLab, reporting hallucinations on 33% of benchmark queries for a Thomson Reuters tool, contrasted with the company's reported internal error rate of 10%. They suggest differences in benchmark construction may explain the discrepancy and explicitly state that the company's undisclosed construction prevents a determination. These figures are distinct from the more than 120 documented court cases involving fabricated citations and law, which are incident counts rather than measured model error rates. The authors also discuss Paxton's advertised 94%+ accuracy, arguing that its selected case-treatment task was too easy to demonstrate broader practical reliability. They cite limited studies and anecdotal reports on human–AI collaboration, without presenting a quantified general productivity effect. Claims about procurement, innovation, competitive advantage, and institutional incentives primarily rest on institutional reasoning. NIST facial-recognition testing, MLPerf, and examples of benchmark gaming in general-purpose AI supply analogies for the proposed arrangements, not direct evidence that those arrangements have already improved legal services. LegalBench is cited as an academic legal-reasoning benchmark; Harvey's BigLaw Bench appears as a vendor benchmark reference, not an independent evaluation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The diagnosis concerns the contemporary transition from research prototypes to deployed legal AI; future benefits and institutional remedies are conditional, without a dated forecast of profession-wide transformation.
pts.d: The supplied article is published July 20, 2026, with many cited sources accessed September 3, 2025. Its assessments of current performance information should be understood in that source context, rather than as independently updated findings. The authors stress that rapid model changes and proliferating tools make comprehensive, current benchmarking difficult. Results are bounded by included tasks, sample construction, protocols, subgroup measures, and deployment conditions. Legal answers can vary across jurisdictions and over time, so reliable benchmarking may require repeated, geographically specific assessment. Their high-resource proposal assumes substantial funding plus legal and technical expertise and envisages recurring in-house benchmarking. The medium-resource proposal assumes capacity to coordinate a consortium, but depends on participation incentives and faces capture, standardization, and sustainability concerns. Under low resources, targeted grants prioritize access-to-justice applications while relinquishing comprehensive market coverage. Predicted consumer benefits depend on demonstrated effectiveness; the article does not forecast a specific date, adoption rate, staffing change, or amount of cost reduction.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The authors identify unequal consequences for legal practitioners and purchasers, vendors, researchers, educators, regulators, and individuals unable to obtain traditional legal assistance.
pts.d: Lawyers need performance information to calibrate reliance and satisfy professional competence obligations; law firms and in-house counsel need it for procurement. Well-resourced firms may gain proprietary advantages from testing, while solo lawyers, nonprofits, and public-interest users risk being underserved by consortia dominated by major firms and transactional work. Smaller vendors can lose opportunities to demonstrate superior performance when benchmark coverage favors incumbents, and their customers remain less informed. Researchers face restricted product and legal-data access, confidentiality constraints, annotation costs, and weak incentives for repeated testing. Law schools and bar associations lack information needed to teach effective use, while courts and legislatures may fall back on coarse disclosure requirements. Individuals seeking help with housing, bankruptcy, or custody have fewer resources to assess chatbot advice; they are the principal intended beneficiaries of the authors' proposed low-resource access-to-justice benchmarking priority.
